prompt: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix: state the space cost of each and the one question that decides which to use.
reveal: Adjacency list is O(V+E); adjacency matrix is O(V²). The deciding question is density: use a matrix only when the graph is dense (E approaches V²) or you need O(1) edge-existence lookups; otherwise use lists. Interview default is lists, since most graphs are sparse.

prompt: When does BFS give you a shortest path and when does it fail? What replaces it when it fails?
reveal: BFS gives shortest paths only when every edge has the same weight — it explores in layers of equal cost. With differing positive weights it fails, and Dijkstra replaces it (swap the queue for a min-heap). With negative edges Dijkstra fails too, and Bellman–Ford handles it.

prompt: Explain topological sort: what must be true of the graph, the two standard algorithms, and how you detect that it is impossible.
reveal: It orders vertices so every edge points forward; it requires a DAG. Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes in-degree-zero nodes with a queue; the DFS method pushes each node onto a stack after its descendants finish, then reverses. Impossible exactly when a cycle exists — Kahn detects it when fewer than V nodes are emitted; DFS detects a back edge to a node still on the recursion stack.

prompt: Why does Dijkstra break with negative edges? Be precise about the invariant that is violated.
reveal: Dijkstra assumes that once a node is popped with the smallest tentative distance, that distance is final — because every remaining path can only add non-negative weight. A negative edge breaks that: a later, longer-looking path can become cheaper after traversing the negative edge, so a finalized node may need updating. Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges V−1 times instead, and a further relaxation on pass V proves a negative cycle.

prompt: Describe union-find with both optimizations and state the resulting complexity. Name two problems where it is the right tool.
reveal: Union by size/rank attaches the smaller tree under the larger, keeping depth low; path compression flattens the path to the root on every find. Together they give near-constant amortized time — the inverse Ackermann function α(n). Right tool for: Kruskal’s MST (detect whether an edge joins two components) and dynamic connectivity / counting connected components as edges arrive.

prompt: Grid BFS with extra state (e.g. fuel, keys, remaining wall-breaks): what goes in the visited set, and what is the pruning invariant?
reveal: The visited set must be keyed on the full state, not just the cell: (row, col, extraState). The pruning invariant is dominance — only revisit a cell if you arrive in a strictly better state (more fuel, more keys, more breaks left); a strictly worse or equal arrival can never lead to a better outcome, so prune it. Store best[r][c] as the best resource seen rather than a plain boolean.

prompt: Kruskal vs Prim for minimum spanning tree: mechanism, data structure, and which you pick when.
reveal: Kruskal sorts all edges and adds the cheapest that does not form a cycle, using union-find — O(E log E), naturally suited to sparse graphs and edge lists. Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always taking the cheapest edge leaving the tree, using a min-heap — O(E log V), better on dense graphs, and structurally almost identical to Dijkstra (the only change is the key: edge weight instead of accumulated distance).

prompt: Many graph problems give you strings, words, or pairs — not integers. Describe the parse → map → algorithm → unmap pattern.
reveal: Step 1 parse: read the input into whatever natural form it comes in (word pairs, course names, ticket routes). Step 2 map: assign each distinct entity an integer id via a hash map, building an adjacency list keyed on ids. Step 3 algorithm: run the standard integer-indexed BFS/DFS/topo-sort/Dijkstra untouched. Step 4 unmap: translate the integer result back to the original labels. Keeping these four steps separate is the whole trick — most bugs come from trying to run the algorithm directly on strings.

prompt: How do you detect a cycle in a DIRECTED graph with DFS, and why does the undirected method fail here?
reveal: Directed: use three colors — white (unvisited), gray (on the current recursion stack), black (fully explored). A cycle exists exactly when you reach a GRAY node, meaning you looped back into the path you are currently on. The undirected method (“found a visited node that is not my parent”) fails for directed graphs because reaching an already-visited BLACK node is perfectly legal — it just means two paths converge, which is not a cycle. The gray/black distinction is what separates “on my current path” from “already done.”

prompt: How do you test whether a graph is bipartite, and what does failure tell you about the graph?
reveal: Two-color the graph with BFS or DFS: assign the start node color 0, and every neighbor the opposite color of the current node. If you ever meet an already-colored neighbor with the SAME color as the current node, it is not bipartite. Failure means the graph contains an ODD-length cycle — that is precisely the characterization: a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle. Remember to loop over all components, since a disconnected graph needs each component tested.

prompt: What is a strongly connected component, and outline how Kosaraju’s algorithm finds them?
reveal: An SCC is a maximal set of vertices where every vertex can reach every other along directed edges. Kosaraju: (1) run DFS on the original graph, pushing each vertex onto a stack when it FINISHES; (2) reverse every edge; (3) pop vertices off the stack and run DFS on the reversed graph — each DFS tree is one SCC. The intuition: finish order approximates a topological order of the components, and reversing edges prevents a DFS from escaping its own component. Condensing each SCC to a single node always yields a DAG.

prompt: 0-1 BFS: what problem does it solve, and why can a deque replace a priority queue?
reveal: It solves shortest paths when every edge weight is either 0 or 1 — common in grid problems where some moves are free and others cost one. Use a deque: relax a 0-weight edge by pushing the neighbor to the FRONT, a 1-weight edge to the BACK. This keeps the deque sorted by distance with at most two distinct values present, which is exactly the ordering a priority queue would maintain — so you get Dijkstra’s correctness at O(V+E) instead of O(E log V).

prompt: What is multi-source BFS and what problem shape signals it?
reveal: Push ALL sources into the queue at distance 0 before starting the BFS, then run one ordinary BFS. The signal: “distance to the NEAREST X” — nearest gate, rotting oranges spreading, distance from every cell to the closest 0. Running a separate BFS per source would be O(sources × (V+E)); seeding them all at once gives the same answer in a single O(V+E) pass, because the wavefront naturally expands from whichever source is closest to each cell.

prompt: Implementing Dijkstra with a binary heap: how do you handle the fact that you cannot decrease-key cheaply?
reveal: The standard trick is LAZY deletion: instead of decreasing a key, push a new (distance, node) pair whenever you improve a distance, allowing duplicates in the heap. When you pop a node, check whether the popped distance is greater than the recorded best — if so, it is a stale entry, so skip it. The heap may hold O(E) entries, giving O(E log E), which is asymptotically equivalent to O(E log V) for simple graphs. Attempting real decrease-key requires an indexed heap and is rarely worth it in an interview.

prompt: When would you use Floyd–Warshall over running Dijkstra from every node? State its structure in one sentence.
reveal: Use it when you need ALL-pairs shortest paths on a small, dense graph (roughly V ≤ 400–500), or when negative edges are present (no negative cycles). Structure: three nested loops with k — the intermediate vertex — as the OUTERMOST, updating dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). O(V³). The loop order matters: k must be outermost so that when you consider it, paths through vertices 1..k-1 are already final. Repeated Dijkstra is better on sparse graphs: O(V × E log V).

prompt: How do you combine topological sort with DP? Give the longest-path-in-a-DAG example.
reveal: Topological order guarantees that when you process a node, every predecessor is already finalized — which is exactly the dependency condition DP needs. Longest path in a DAG: topologically sort, then relax in that order: for each node u in topo order, for each edge u→v, dp[v] = max(dp[v], dp[u] + w(u,v)). O(V+E). This is worth internalizing because longest path is NP-hard in general graphs but linear-time on a DAG — acyclicity is what buys you the DP. Course scheduling, build ordering, and DAG path counting all use this shape.

prompt: Connected components: when do you use union-find instead of DFS/BFS?
reveal: Use DFS/BFS when the graph is given up front and static — it is simpler and O(V+E). Use union-find when edges ARRIVE INCREMENTALLY and you must answer connectivity queries as they come, or when the problem is fundamentally about merging groups (Kruskal, accounts-merge, number-of-islands-with-streaming-additions). Union-find handles online merging in near-constant time; redoing a DFS after every edge would be O(E × (V+E)). Union-find cannot handle edge DELETION, which is a common follow-up trap.

prompt: How does A* differ from Dijkstra, and what property must the heuristic satisfy?
reveal: A* prioritizes nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n): the known cost so far plus an ESTIMATE of the remaining cost, so search is pulled toward the goal instead of expanding uniformly in all directions. Dijkstra is the special case h = 0. The heuristic must be ADMISSIBLE — never overestimating the true remaining cost — or A* can return a suboptimal path. For grids, Manhattan distance (4-directional) or Euclidean (free movement) are the standard admissible choices.

prompt: A 2D grid is a graph. State the implicit vertex set, edge set, and the one line of code that generates neighbors.
reveal: Vertices are the cells (r, c); edges connect orthogonally (or diagonally) adjacent walkable cells. Neighbors come from a direction array: for (dr, dc) in [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)], neighbor = (r+dr, c+dc), guarded by bounds and walkability checks. Recognizing that no explicit adjacency list is needed — the grid IS the graph, generated on the fly — is the unlock for the entire grid-BFS family.

prompt: What are the conditions for an Eulerian path and an Eulerian circuit? Contrast with Hamiltonian.
reveal: Eulerian path (uses every EDGE exactly once) exists in a connected undirected graph when zero or exactly two vertices have odd degree; if zero, it is an Eulerian circuit. Directed version: every vertex has in-degree equal to out-degree for a circuit, or exactly one vertex with out−in = 1 and one with in−out = 1 for a path. Hamiltonian (every VERTEX exactly once) has no such simple characterization and is NP-complete — that contrast (edges easy, vertices hard) is the point worth remembering.

prompt: You ran BFS/Dijkstra and have distances. How do you RECONSTRUCT the actual path?
reveal: Maintain a parent (predecessor) array during the search: whenever you relax an edge into v via u, set parent[v] = u. Afterwards, walk backwards from the target through parent until you reach the source, then reverse the list. Cost is O(path length) and one extra array. The common mistake is only tracking distances and then trying to rebuild the path by re-deriving it afterward — always record the predecessor as you go.

prompt: Why is a minimum spanning tree NOT the same as a shortest-path tree? Give the intuition.
reveal: An MST minimizes the TOTAL weight of edges connecting all vertices; a shortest-path tree minimizes the distance FROM ONE SOURCE to every other vertex. They optimize different objectives, so a path in an MST between two nodes can be far longer than the true shortest path. Intuition: the MST cares about global cheapness of the network; Dijkstra cares about egocentric distance from a chosen root.
